title: Molecular heterogeneity of the non-human primate cochlea

paper_content.abstract: Unraveling the intricate composition and function of the cochlea is paramount to comprehending the mechanisms underlying sound perception and the pathogenesis of auditory disorders. The mammalian cochlea displays a highly organized structure, which contributes to the diversity and complexity of auditory processing. However, the cellular intricacies in non-human primates remain largely unexplored. In the present study, we employed high-throughput transcriptomic sequencing to profile over 36,701 nuclei across virtually all cochlear cell types in both juvenile and adult Macaca fascicularis at single-cell resolution. Our analysis unveiled remarkable heterogeneity both across and within cell types. Despite a largely conserved cellular composition of the cochlea between mouse and macaque species, glial cells exhibited substantial species-specific diversity, while hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons with specialized transcriptional programs were well-mapped onto their murine counterparts, underscoring the similarities that persist despite evolutionary divergence. Furthermore, we constructed a disease map associated with hearing loss, establishing this transcriptomic atlas of the macaque cochlea as an indispensable resource for future investigations in both human and non-human primates.
paper_content.introduction:
The cochlea, a coiled structure situated in the inner ear, performs unique biophysical functions in vertebrates and serves as the primary sound transducer. Airborne pressure waves induce fluid-based traveling waves at the base of the cochlea, which propagate towards the apex within the scala vestibuli. These waves progressively vibrate the spiral duct in the scala media and subsequently travel back toward the base in the scala tympani1. During this complex fluctuation process, the sensory epithelium lining the floor of the scala media, known as the cochlear epithelium, perceives mechanical stimuli and transduces physical signals to neurons2. The cochlear epithelium comprises two types of mechanosensory hair cells (HCs), namely inner HCs and outer HCs, and at least six types of associated glia-like supporting cells (SCs). The scarcity of HCs and SCs in mammals, with approximately 700 inner HCs and 2000 outer HCs in mice3, and around 15,000 HCs in the human cochlea3, poses significant challenges in investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying the development and physiology of this organ. Furthermore, the vulnerability and sensitivity of cochlear cells, particularly those in the epithelial tissue, coupled with the calcification of the temporal bone in juvenile and adult stages, render cochlear dissection an exceptionally arduous task.

Damage or degeneration of the cochlea can lead to irreversible HC loss in mammals4,5, with hereditary hearing loss (HL) being the most common disabling sensorineural disorder. The majority of genes known to be associated with deafness are expressed in specific cochlear cell types, such as HCs, and these genes often affect the mechanoelectrical transduction components in the hair bundles that are critical for sound perception, including Cib2 (calcium and integrin-binding family member 2), Tmie (transmembrane protein), and Tmc1/2 (transmembrane channel-like protein 1/2). Other genes, such as GJB2 (connexin-26), are expressed in several types of SCs6. However, a comprehensive disease map of deafness genes in non-human primates remains elusive. Gene therapy strategies, primarily based on the adeno-associated virus delivery system, are increasingly being tested in mouse models that mimic human deafness. Nevertheless, it is imperative to optimize the safety and efficacy of gene therapies in larger animal models, such as non-human primates, for advanced preclinical trials due to species-specific differences in physiology and anatomy between mice and humans.

Over the past two decades, developmental biologists have made significant strides in uncovering the cellular and genetic processes that regulate the formation of this remarkable structure, including the major axes of cochlear development7,8, HC fate determination and trans-differentiation9,10, and the identification and function of the mechanoelectrical transduction complex11,12. In rodents, the sensory epithelium and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) remain immature prior to and at birth, undergoing remodeling and maturation around postnatal days (P) 2113,14, concurrent with the regression of the greater epithelial ridge, detachment of the tectorial membrane, and the formation of the endocochlear potential15,16. Recent advances in microfluidic-based single-cell/single-nucleus transcriptomic approaches, which enable the capture of large numbers of cells, have facilitated the development of cell atlases of the mouse cochlea from embryonic to adult stages17–19. However, a comprehensive cell transcriptomic atlas of the cochlea in non-human primates has yet to be undertaken20. Given their evolutionary proximity to humans, constructing a non-human primate cell atlas as a reference for the cochlea is a critical step in advancing our understanding of human auditory physiology, disease, and aging.

In the present study, we utilized juvenile and adult Macaca fascicularis cochleae to generate a high-quality single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas. This map revealed remarkable cellular diversity in the spiral ganglion region, particularly among glial cells. Furthermore, we identified conserved and divergent features between the mouse and macaque cochlea. We anticipate that this atlas will be invaluable for understanding evolutionary innovations in the mammalian cochlea and for developing organoid models and gene therapy of human diseases associated with deafness.
paper_content.results:
A cell type atlas of the macaque cochlea
To determine the cellular composition of the macaque cochlea, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; Droplet-based 10× Genomics) on 36,701 nuclei after quality control, doublet removal, and filtering (Fig. 1a–d and Supplementary Fig. 1a–c; for details see “Method”). We profiled the entire cochlea, with nuclei sampled from the cochlear epithelium, spiral ganglion, stria vascularis, spiral ligament, and other tissues, including macrophages and pericytes, in a 1-, 5-, and 11-year-old macaques across approximately juvenile and adult stages (Supplementary Figs. 1–3b, c).

To fine-tune the characterization of macaque cochlear cell types, we first utilized the published single-nucleus and single-cell transcriptome of murine cochleae as a reference for assessing well-established marker genes used for manual cell-type annotation (Supplementary Fig. 4). These gene markers used in the referenced dataset have been thoroughly validated in the murine cochlea across juvenile and adult periods19. We found that our in-house single-nucleus sequencing data of the murine cochlea at P25 exhibited approximately similar cellular diversity comparable to the referenced dataset from Jean et al.19 (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6) and observed accurate cell-type mapping onto our macaque cochleae (Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Figs. 1d, e, g, h and 2a, b). However, some differences exist as circulating cells including erythrocytes, neutrophils, B cells, T cells, NK cells, monocytes, and mast cells are undetectable in our in-house dataset compared to Jean et al.’s dataset19 (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Figs. 1, 2 and 5). We reasoned that it is likely due to cochlear dissection process for single-nucleus suspension we used, which was different from Jean et al.19.

By using a support vector machine classifier trained on the macaque cells, we find strong correspondence between the transcriptomic signatures of the sensory organ cell types in macaques and mice underscoring a highly conserved molecular identity between macaque and murine species (Supplementary Fig. 3d), as well as high quality and accuracy within these cell types (Supplementary Figs. 1f, i, 2c, and 5c, g). Moreover, our atlas also displays five main cell-type ensembles (Supplementary Fig. 3c) as noted previously19. The cell ensembles of the neurosensory epithelium, for instance, consist of SCs (defined by OTOG expression) and HCs (defined by MYO7A expression; Supplementary Fig. 3c). For further validation of these sequencing data, we applied immunofluorescence assays to confirm the localization of selectively the most differentially expressed genes. CALB1 encoding calbindin, a hair cell marker9, is localized in both inner and outer HCs. Otoferlin (OTOF), an inner HC marker21, is exclusively present in inner HCs when HCs become mature. CALB2 encoding calretinin, a calcium-binding protein, is illustrated as localized in SGNs22–24. All these immunolabeling experiments also exhibited similar cell-type-specific localization in both species (Fig. 1f). Furthermore, RNAscopeTM in situ hybridization also confirm the spatial expression patterns of ANXA1 in root cells and spindle cells as well as OTOGL in HCs and SCs (Supplementary Fig. 3a).

Furthermore, we were able to map the unique biological functions of each cell type via gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of these highly variable genes (Supplementary Data 1), revealing remarkably similar biological functions across species. For example, sensory processing of sound mapped to HCs, actin filament-based processes to SCs, modulation of chemical synaptic transmission to SGNs, myelination to Schwann cells, and cell junction organization to marginal stria cells. Collectively, we constructed an accessible cellular taxonomy of the juvenile and adult macaque cochlea, revealing an evolutionarily conserved, highly specialized sensory organ across mammalian species based on a clustering analysis for identifying cell types of cochlear cells using the expression of canonical marker genes in mice.

Auditory receptors in macaque cochlea
HCs with unique mechanical sensory properties in the auditory system play a crucial role in sound transduction. To gain comprehensive insights into their molecular identities compared to mouse species, we integrated our macaque and mouse single-nucleus data separately using the single-cell variational inference (scVI) method25 (Supplementary Fig. 6) and subset the HC population based on the unique expression of the HC marker MYO7A/Myo7a (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). We observed a strong correspondence between the transcriptomic signatures of the HC lineages in macaques and mice, as mature/terminal marker genes26–28 (OHC: SLC26A5/Slc26a5, KCNQ4/Kcnq4 and PCP4/Ocm; IHC: SLC17A8/Slc17a8, CALB2/Calb2, and ATP2A3/Atp2a3) are selectively enriched in these two subtypes (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 7). The motor protein PRESTIN was precisely localized in the OHC basolateral membrane in both species (Fig. 2b, c and Supplementary Fig. 7) and OHCs in macaque species exhibited the biophysical feature of motility evoked by electrical stimuli (Fig. 2d and Movie S1). Furthermore, well-characterized transcriptional regulators that specify and maintain the fate of OHCs and IHCs, including IKZF29 (which encodes IKAROS family zinc finger 2) and TBX210,29 (which encodes T-box transcription factor 2), were strongly expressed in HCs across species (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 7). These findings suggest that HCs in the cochlea of both species might share conserved gene regulatory machinery.

Glial cell diversity in the macaque cochlea
In the mouse cochlea, glial cells exhibit spatial and functional heterogeneity and can be categorized into three distinct subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 8): satellite glial cells (SGSs), myelinating Schwann cells (MSCs), and non-myelinating Schwann cells (NMSCs). Unique marker genes for these subtypes have been well-established in mice30. To investigate this diversity in the macaque cochlea, we sub-clustered glial cells into three subtypes (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 8c). Similar to murine glial types, macaque glial cells displayed region-specific differences in the spiral ganglion region, including cells enveloping sensory neurons (SGCs), cells wrapping around axons forming myelin (MSCs), and Remak bundles (NMSCs), as demonstrated by immunostaining of the pan-glial marker MBP for glial localization (Fig. 3b, c). However, we were unable to map macaque glial subtypes using several defined markers (SCN7A, encoding an atypical Na-sensitive Na-channel that marks NMSCs30,31; NCAMP, encoding a non-compact myelin-associated protein that marks MSCs30,32; and IGFBP6, encoding the insulin-like growth factor binding protein 6 that marks SGCs30) that have been validated in mice30 (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 8b and d). To further harmonize both species’ glial subtypes, we changed different highly variable genes (hvgs) imputed for anchoring and found that varying the number of hvgs did not affect the species or cell-type mixings in the manifold embedding spaces, and we still obtained a relatively stable high-level structure for the data manifold (Supplementary Fig. 9a–c). This might suggest that there is relatively high transcriptomic divergence in peripheral glial cell types between macaques and mice. Indeed, these cluster pairs showed relatively low classification accuracy with various cells showing overlaps (Supplementary Fig. 9d) as well as cell mixing upon multiple integrative method we used for cross-species integration (Supplementary Fig. 10). For example, we found that the pan-astrocyte marker GFAP showed region-specific localization in mouse MSCs but was more diverse in macaque glial cells, including cells engulfing SGNs and cells parallel to axons (Fig. 3e).

In the central nervous system (CNS), astrocytes play auxiliary roles in neuron development, synapse formation and elimination, potassium homeostasis, and blood-brain barrier function33–35. A recent single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of the peripheral sensory system revealed that glial cells in the mouse cochlea share many core glial signature genes with radial glial cells and astrocytes in the CNS30. To explore potential functional implications, we plotted genes associated with astrocyte function and compared the molecular profiles of glial cells in both species (Fig. 3f). Our analysis revealed several apparent species-specific gene expression patterns related to astrocyte functions. For instance, glial cells in mice showed predominant expression of Na+-K+-ATPase channels (higher levels of ATP1B1, ATP1A1, and ATP1A2), while glial subtypes in macaques displayed higher levels of glutamate receptors (GRIA2 and GR1K2), potentially associated with potassium buffering. Regarding debris clearance, CLU36 and LRP137 were more prominently expressed in macaque glial cells, while MEGF1037 and MERTK37 were more abundant in mouse glial cells. Consistent with these findings, our RNAscopeTM results suggest that peripheral glial cells in macaque could be divided into two main types (Fig. 3j): GRIA2-positive SGSs predominantly located in the modiolus region (Fig. 3g), and CLU-/GRIA2-positive or CLU-positive Schwann cells distributed along the outer modiolar region as neuronal fibers project into both cochlear epithelium (Fig. 3h) and cochlear nuclei (Fig. 3i). These spatial distributions were generally consistent with the sequencing data showing widespread GRIA2 expression in macaque glial cells and selective CLU enrichment in GC_1/GC_3 clusters (Fig. 3f).

While we observed differences in gene expression patterns between species, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the technical limitations of snRNA sequencing. Further validation would be needed to determine whether these molecular differences reflect genuine functional divergence in cochlear glial cells across species.

Sensory neuron diversity in the macaque cochlea
We next investigated the diversity of SGNs. Defined by canonical markers in mice23,24 (Supplementary Fig. 11), 955 SGNs in macaques can be re-clustered into type I/II subclasses and subdivided into four subtypes with distinct expression patterns (Fig. 4a, b and Supplementary Fig. 12). However, subtle differences were observed in macaque sensory neurons (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 12c). TH expression was preferentially enriched only in mouse type II neurons, and the type IC marker genes POU4F1 and LYPD1 were specifically expressed in mouse type IC neurons. Interestingly, we found that, unlike mouse SGNs, expression of the type IB marker CALB1 was enriched in macaque type II neurons (Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Fig. 13). Immunolabeling of CALB1 with type II markers, including GATA3 and PRPH proteins, confirmed that CALB1 protein is co-localized with these two type II SGN markers, indicating that CALB1 is a macaque-specific marker for type II sensory neurons (Fig. 4d).

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis identified a cohort of conserved transcription factors (TFs) that were share either in type I or type II SGNs in both species (Fig. 4e, g). Among them, some have been previously reported, such as PROX138, RUNX139, and SMAD122. For example, RUNX1 is essential for type IC SGN specification. Immunolabeling and RNASCOPE assay confirmed these TFs selectively expressed in SGN subtypes (Fig. 4f, h). Additionally, we found primate-specific TFs PBX3 particularly expressed in type II SGNs (Fig. 4i). Gene set enrichment analysis showed that the key TF PBX3 is involved in GO terms related to neuron development (Fig. 4j). Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that the PBX3 protein is localized in the cell nucleus of macaque SGNs, probably as a specific subtype, but not in mouse SGNs (Fig. 4k). However, future experiments should be conducted to determine if PBX3 plays primate-specific roles in SGNs.

The similarity and specificity of expression profiles in the cochlear epithelium
We focused on the cochlear epithelium, also known as the organ of Corti, which is a highly specialized structure for sound detection and transduction40–42. To explore cross-species similarities and differences in the cochlear epithelium at different taxonomic levels, we employed mutiple label-transfer algorithms (scVI, CCA, and Symphany) to integrate our in-house mouse cochlear epithelium clusters as references and projected the 10, 870 macaque single-nucleus transcriptomes onto them based on their distances in their joint-embedding spaces (Fig. 5a, b and Supplementary Fig. 14; see “Methods”), resulting in highly overlapped anchoring identity (Fig. 5c). Additionally, label transfer-based integrated cell types exhibited highly similar transcriptomes (Fig. 5d, e) though we found CC_ISC_OSC and IBC_IPh_HeC varied across species, suggesting their species-specificity.

Further analysis of the expression of gene families across cluster pairs indicated that, as demonstrated in other systems43–45, certain families, such as G protein-coupled receptors and TFs (especially the zinc finger types), displayed cell type-specific expression patterns in the cochlear epithelium (Fig. 5f, g). This suggests that zinc finger type TFs might function as markers of cochlear epithelium identity in both species. Indeed, our immunolabeling or RNAscopeTM assay of selective TFs (GATA3, IKZF2, PBX3, and NR2F2) showed similar expression patterns across species (Fig. 5h, i). However, a supervised learning task for testing the ability of gene-sets related to signaling, ion channels, and cell adhesion to distinguish cochlear epithelium consensus types showed similar classification performance when trained and tested within species (r-value greater than 1.12) but declined sharply across species (60% in macaques and mice; Fig. 5j). Altogether, these results indicate that evolutionary conservation might be maintained by combined TF codes, while species-specific adaptation might be driven by species-enriched genes (either TFs or effector genes).

Mapping deafness-associated genes across species
To further examine our dataset and gain deep insights into the cross-species expression profile of genes related to hereditary hearing loss (HHL), we mapped HHL-related genes (https://hereditaryhearingloss.org, updated on 02/17/2022) categorized into four types: autosomal dominant nonsyndromic HL (48 genes), autosomal recessive nonsyndromic HL (74 genes), syndromic HL (41 genes), and X-linked nonsyndromic/age/noise/cisplatin-related HL (46 genes) in our databases for systematic characterization of their expression profiles. It is important to note that genes linked to age, noise, and cisplatin-related HL by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have not been extensively investigated in the inner ear (GWAS Catalog (ebi.ac.uk)). Through the overall examination of HL-related gene expression in the macaque, we observed that the majority of these genes exhibit cell-type-specific expression patterns (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 15). For instance, POU4F3—a well-established deafness gene—is predominantly expressed in HCs, with its mutations known to cause DFNA15, a common autosomal dominant hearing loss disorder. The gene Gjb2, which encodes connexin 26 for gap junctions, is broadly expressed in SCs and cells of the lateral wall. Mutations in Gjb2 are associated with both congenital HL and later-onset deafness. Notably, our data demonstrate highly conserved expression patterns across 1-, 5-, and 11-year-old macaques, further validating the robustness of our dataset. Cross-species comparative analysis reveals that deafness-associated genes are evolutionarily conserved between macaques and mice, sharing analogous expression profiles. Together, this analysis revealed the cross-species distributions of HL-related genes within the whole cochlear map. Given the close evolutionary proximity of macaque to humans, establishing this atlas holds significant implications for advancing research on human auditory pathologies.
paper_content.methods:
Animals and ethical compliance
All experiments involving macaques (Macaca fascicularis) were conducted in strict accordance with the guidelines set forth by the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International (AAALAC) for the ethical treatment of non-human primates. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the ethical committee of the State Key Laboratory of Primate Biomedical Research. For the purpose of single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), cochleae from one 1-year-old male, two 5-year-old male, and one 11-year-old female macaque were utilized. Immunostaining experiments were performed using cochleae from three 5-year-old male and one 11-year-old male macaque. Electromotility recordings were obtained from one 1-year-old male macaque. All animals were housed in facilities that meet the standards of the AAALAC, and their well-being was closely monitored throughout the study.

C57BL/6J mice used in this study were purchased from GenePharmtech Co., Ltd. and housed in a standard specific pathogen free environment. Mice of either sex aged postnatal days 21 to 25 were used in this study with no obvious sex phenotype observed. All mice were housed under controlled conditions, including room temperature (23±3°C), relative humidity (55±5%), and a 12-h light/dark cycle. During the feeding process, all mice were provided with sterile water and nutrient-balanced feed. Additionally, each cage was equipped with non-toxic and harmless bedding.

Macaque RNA-seq, quality control, and clustering
Sample collection. For single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), juvenile and adult macaques were deeply anesthetized with ketamine (10 mg/kg) and perfused with cold artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) following the cessation of the pedal withdrawal reflex. The entire inner ear was rapidly extracted, and the cochlea was carefully dissected and embedded in chilled DMEM medium. During dissection, the outer bones encasing the cochlear duct were meticulously removed using surgical forceps under a dissection microscope. To obtain a comprehensive representation of cell types, care was taken to slightly remove the outer bones attached to the lateral wall of the cochlea. The entire cochlear duct was then transferred into a 1.5 ml tube, quickly frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C until nuclei isolation. Both cochleae from each animal were collected.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Chen et al. present a cross-species comparative study between mouse and macaque cochlear cell types. They profil more than 20643 nuclei from 1-year old and 11-year old crab-eating macaque cochlea, and 9470 nuclei from P21-25 murine cochlea using single-nucleus RNA sequencing on the 10x chromium platform. Nuclei were collected from cochlear epithelium, spiral ganglion, stria vascularis, spiral ligament, and other inner ear components including Reissner’s membrane, macrophages and osteoblasts. Through a series of computational comparative analyses, the authors demonstrat conserved and divergent features between mouse and macaque cochlea and cellular diversity in spiral ganglion neurons. This cochlear snRNAseq dataset from non-human primates is a tremendous feat and ultimately a step closer to understanding the pathophysiology of the inner ear in mammals. However, unfortunately the manuscript in its current form has some major issues that do not make it acceptable for publication.

Major concerns:
1. Writing composition: Throughout the manuscript, there are innumerable grammatical and syntax errors that make reading it quite laborious. This reviewer initially began keeping track of these, but quickly became overwhelmed with this effort. I do suggest that the authors take a careful look at their writing.
2. Validation of results: There is sparce validation data for most of the manuscript. While there is one transcription factor that the authors validate as unique to the macaque (PBX3), there is none for the major cell types of the organ of Corti such as inner or out hair cells, or any of the supporting cell types. Without such validation, it is unclear if any of the presented data is biologically relevant.
3. A recent comprehensive snRNAseq dataset from Jean et al. (2023, PNAS) has 37 cell types described in mouse, with several of the cell types described (and validated) there not present in the dataset here. Any thoughts on the discrepancy here? Would using that now publicly available dataset provide a better comparison (at least the P20 data)?
4. Figures 1-5 lack some originality in presenting the data. Certain parts of the manuscript are a near complete recapitulation of Bakken et al., 2021 (Nature), including to the level of figure colors (e.g. Fig 3d here and Fig 2c in Bakken et al, among others).
5. I understand and appreciate that obtaining inner samples from macaques is difficult for a variety of reasons. However, there is a vast age difference between the two animals used here (1 year old and 11 year old). It would be much more convincing if there was a closer age match – for example two 1 year old or two 11 year old animals. Furthermore, in Fig 1b, there appears to be a couple of large groups of cells that are only in the 1yo macaque, and not the 11 year old. This is either batch effect or related to age differences. If related to age differences, then at least one additional specimen is needed per category. These cells groups are later labeled as Fibro2 and Fibro4_RMC.
6. Cell composition analysis (Fig 1e) cannot be inferred from percentages. This is not computationally sound. See (https://www.sc-best-practices.org/conditions/compositional.html) for details and explanation. This figure should either be removed or performed in a computationally rigorous manner.
7. How many hair cells of each sub-type are in the two datasets (mouse and macaque)? Did the authors make any attempt to harvest a larger number of hair cell nuclei? And why are the IHCs and OHCs so far apart on the UMAP? In nearly every other manuscript with scRNAseq from the inner ear, they’re not that far apart in space. I understand that relation of cells cannot be fully inferred from UMAP, but I have not seen these cell types this far apart on a UMAP.
8. Re Fig 5d: Calb1 and Calb2 differences between mouse and macaque is not obvious here. Any attempts at quantification? That would be more convincing. It would be even more convincing if there was some in situ hybridization with quantification.
9. Did the authors pull out any tonotopic data? There’s discussion of the hearing frequency differences between mouse and macaque, but is there any tonotopic evidence computationally in either the mouse and/or the macaque data?
10. The authors do not use a robust computational method for their chosen clustering resolution. It would behoove the authors to clearly perform a calculation to determine the optimal clustering for each of their datasets. For example, Bakken et al 2021 have a method to do this, and there are a few other methods available in the literature (e.g. Patterson-Cross et al., 2021, BMC Bioinformatics).
11. Methodology: there’s a clear lack of details in the methods regarding how tissue was obtained in the macaque. Description of the dissection technique is lacking, what enzymes were used for dissociation and for how long, time from animal sacrifice to loading on the 10x Controller, etc…
12. Code availability: without proper and detailed code (for example shared on GitHub or similar platform), this reviewer cannot clearly see what was done from a computational perspective. While there are descriptions of all of the steps, and references to others who have done similar work, this is not a substitute for clear and well-annotated code for both peer-review and for the general scientific audience.
13. I have some concerns regarding the consistency of what is said and what is shown. For example, throughout the main manuscript, the authors refer to a 1 year old macaque, however, in the supplementals (Fig S1d), they write "Macaque_8M" a number of times. Is it 1 year old or 8 month old?
14. Where are the inner/outer hair cells in Figure S4a? I only see “HC” as a category without determination of IHC/OHCs. If there’s claims of translational potential, it would be critical to rigorously show both inner and outer hair cell composition along with appropriate validation of these cell types. There’s discussion of this work being important for pathological conditions such as age related hearing loss (ARHL). Approximately 80% of ARHL is secondary to cochlear hair cell loss.

Minor concerns:
1. Abstract: The last sentence mentions human stem cell-based models of disease. However, there’s no data or any reference to stem cells anywhere else in the manuscript.
2. Introduction: line 92- reference is missing
3. Introduction: line 97-99- meaning is not clear
4. Introduction: line 106 and 109- the full forms of MET and AAV should be mentioned when the term is first introduced
5. Results: line 193- typo: ‘uncvered’
6. Manuscript should say “glia” or “glial cells” not “glia cells”
7. Did the authors attempt another species comparison method?
8. Line 363-364: the human hearing frequency should be listed (20Hz to 20,000Hz).
9. Fig1a: Cartoon should not read “aged” macaque but “adult” macaque.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Although it is of significance to reveal the cell composition and function diversity of non-human primate cochlea, and this study constructed a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the macaque cochlea and discovered remarkable heterogeneity across and within cell types, this work is still rudimentary, requires a lot of follow-up work to improve.
1. The purpose of this study is to construct a single-cell atlas of the cochlea in non-human primates. However, the authors selected only one male individual aged 1 year and one female individual aged 11 years of the crab-eating macaque species for single-cell sequencing. Due to a great variation between individuals, the quantity of samples at the same gender and the same age in biological studies is generally more than 3. In order to avoid the effects of individual differences on the results, the authors should increase the samples for sequencing. It would be difficult to get the manuscript published in a decent journal like Nature Communications if the issue was not resolved.
2. Aging and sex itself must have a significant effect on the gene expression of the cochlea, how can the authors rule out the impact of age? In particular, there are obvious differences in the age of the individuals used in the manuscript.
3. In Figure 2B, it is evident that Fibro 2, Fibro4_RMC, and other cell types are predominantly found in the 1-year-old crab-eating monkey but not in 11-year-old monkey. Since the 1-year-old macaque is still at the developmental stage, this observation strongly suggests either a pronounced individual heterogeneity or potential developmental transition from the juvenile to the adult stage in the crab-eating monkey cochlea. Selecting sexually mature crab-eating macaque individual would be required. Similarly, the authors used the mice of the age of P21-25, more samples at different age and both genders are required.
4. The authors mentioned in the Ethical compliance section that there were 1-, 5-, and 11-year-old crab-eating monkey cochleae used for single-cell nuclear sequencing, but the data of 5-year-old sample was not found in the manuscript. The scientific rigor of the paper needs to be ensured.
5. The numbers of captured hair cells and SGNs are quite small. The authors should probe the diversity of hair cells, which is one of the most important cells of the cochlea. More analysis and related experimental validation are required.
6. More details about the steps for isolation of cochlear single cell nuclei should be provided.
7. This manuscript is very descriptive without a focused point or pathway. The authors are suggested to perform an in-depth analysis into the bioinformatic data, and more validation experiments are required. For example, the authors found that USH2A is highly expressed in the cochlear hair cells of monkeys. To make the results more convincing, IHC, IF, single cell-based qPCR should be performed. Further, to explore the role of USH2A, both loss of function and gain of function experiments in primary monkey cells are required.
8. The author employed the biomaRt package for the homology gene conversion between crab-eating macaques and mice. However, using the human genome as an intermediate reference is not an optimal approach. Unlike the well-annotated reference genome in mice, the integrity of the macaque MF 5.0 reference genome seems relatively poor, with many genes lacking complete annotations. Consequently, biomaRt fails to perform homology annotation for these unannotated genes. Moreover, the author utilized the human genome as an intermediary and employed biomaRt (version: 2.42.1) with the Macaca_fascicularis_6.0 reference genome, which further amplifies errors in homology annotation. A more appropriate alternative would involve directly performing BLAST sequence alignment between crab-eating macaques and mouse. In addition, the authors are suggested to provide the list of homolog genes between crab-eating macaques and mouse.
9. In Fig. S18, in order to construct heatmaps of all subclasses of hearing loss genes, the authors subsampled 10 nuclei from each species. However, analyzing subclasses with a higher proportion in the population resulted in significant information loss. To reduce such noise, utilizing a sampling method with replacement might be a preferable choice.
10. It is a lack of details of the computational approaches and the code should be provided on the GitHub page.
11. A statistical approach to identify the appropriate resolution or find the number of clusters should be performed. There are a variety of packages can be used (i.e. see Patterson‐Cross et al 2021 PMID: 33522897).
12. The number of cells for each cell group and each sample should be clearly annotated.

Minor points:
1. The authors need to explain "less than 15,000 genes" (lines 543 and 566) in the QC process.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
‘Xin Chen et al.’ present in their paper a cellular map of the macaque cochlea at the single cell level and provide transcriptomic signatures for all the cell types they detected. To the best of my knowledge, it is the first time that a primate single cell transcriptome of the cochlea is proposed and has the potential to be highly valuable for the whole cochlear and auditory neuroscience field. The major therapy approach currently explored for genetic forms of deafness is gene therapy. Tens of preclinical studies in the mouse have or are currently investigating therapeutic approaches and strategies for many deafness genes. These therapeutic approaches to be safe need well designed promoters to ensure that the therapeutic cassettes target only the relevant cell types. This is one reason why there has now been a number of single cell transcriptomic studies in the mouse. In the view of translating these gene therapies from mice to humans, a single cell transcriptomic dataset in a non-human primate is essential to make sure the gene therapies designed in mice have a chance to be safe and to be rapidly translated to patients. It is in this context that ‘Xin Chen et al.’ provide a macaque transcriptomic single cell atlas of the cochlea based on the analysis of 20 600 nuclei. The authors have carried out their project using states of the art single cell sequencing techniques and analysis tools. Despite the quality of the data processing and graphical presentation, the manuscript presents several issues including two major ones, a) the low quality of English and b) the fact that the manuscript does not add much to the cochlear transcriptomic knowledge in the current state.

i) English. It is a shame that the authors did not use professional services from native scientific English speakers. The manuscript seems to be a direct translation of a foreign language using online tools. The consequences are the presence of many sentences with wrong grammar/syntax, the impossibility to understand some sentences (sometimes whole paragraphs), and probably many misunderstandings including in my assessment of the data. Here are just a few illustrations of the many issues:
-approximate wording: the title wording is unclear, what is a ‘spiral ganglion hub’ (line 149), to ‘attach small portion of oligodendrocytes’ should read ‘to collect’ (line157), what is a ‘high specialized terminator?’ (line 220),
-Coordinating conjunctions are often place at the start of sentences like ‘And’ (lines 154, 185,196).
-Whole paragraphs are hardly understandable (ex: lines 209-214)
-Major misunderstanding. The authors use the word ‘diversity for cell types’, which suggests that there are more cell types in the macaque than in the mouse like among glial cells. In fact, it seems that there are as many cell types. Rather, the macaque glial cells display more differentially expressed genes compared to mouse glial cells than in any other cochlear cell type (see abstract, paragraph from line 254).

ii) A general impression emerges that the conclusions are not drawn to the full potential of the data. There are of course many similarities between mouse and macaque. The authors try to pinpoint the differences. However, they seem to be of a limited impact and/or they are not confirmed with alternative techniques. Apart for PBX3, the other detected molecular claims have not been confirmed by another approach. For example, RNAscope, that is a robust mRNA detection technique could be used on a few precious macaque slices in some instances to confirm the hypothesis made by the authors. This concerns Transcription factor differences claims and glial cell expression differences between the mouse and macaque. In addition, the molecular calb1 marker difference could be of great importance in the auditory neuropathy field. In this field, it is of great debate whether the categorization of auditory nerve neurons found in rodents (low, middle and high threshold neurons) exist in primates and even more in humans. One would expect to see more explorations of this aspect using RNAscope or any other comparable method that is ethically compatible with the use of macaques.

One consequence of this lack of data confirmation is that the many form conclusions cannot be drawn. Here are a couple of examples:
-line 200: “these results suggest that a cohort fo TFs and effector genes can be used to classify cochlear cell types, but further verification is needed…”
-line288: “Future experiments should determine if these genes differed in species…”
-line 319: “ However, future experiments should determine…”.
-line 384, conclusion of the manuscript: “Different datasets, however, may require particular or combinatorial batch-corrected methods, since too strong correction might eliminate hidden variations in intro- or inter-species.”

iii) There are several generic conclusions that would deserve discussion. For example, I respectfully disagree with this affirmation: “By contrast, divergences across species provide strong evidence for adaptation or drift of non-human primate cochlea function, and of susceptibility to human-specific diseases”. There are of course difference in expression patterns of genes between different species. In several instances of the manuscript, the authors seem to want to push this idea that should be discussed in a more balanced way. The authors should give precise examples of human-specific diseases. To which ones do they refer? If one considers genetic forms of deafness for example, more than 150 genes have been identified. To the best of my knowledge, all of these genetic forms of deafness have been replicated either from human to mouse or from mouse to human. Moreover, there are more and more examples of particular audiological signatures associated with specific genetic forms of deafness that have been uncovered in mice and that were confirmed subsequently in patients. So there is clearly a very close resemblance in the genetic architecture and function of mouse and human cochleas. This does not necessarily mean of course that the transcriptomes are identical but it is important to address whether the differences observed in the manuscript may endanger or not the direct translation of therapies from mice to humans.

iv) Several methodological aspects were unclear:
-how many macaque cochleas were used in each sample? How many macaque replicates? It is likely that very few replicates were used for obvious reasons. However, this means that the differentially expressed genes between mouse have to be considered with care and require complemnetary methods (see point iii) above)
-the methods mention 1, 5, and 11 year old macaques. Are the macaques systematically mixed? Are there analysis between 1, 5, and 11 year old macaques.
-Only nuclei with more than 15000 genes were filtered out. This number seems very high and increases the risk of analyzing duplicates and or cells for which both the nuclear and cytosolic transcriptome were caught. A number like 5000 would be more reasonnable.
-Did the authors detect non circulating cells (lymphocites, macrophages etc…)? Were they filtered out during the procedure? How many out of the 20000 nuclei were finally exploited for the data presentation?

Minor issues.
i) Several sentences in the manuscript are not informative or lack relevance.
ii) Figures are generally well made. However, several problems need to be solves:
-many panels are unreadable due to too small characters (ex Fig. 1C, colour code about the nodes are unreadable in 2b,the colour codes for the cell types in the heat maps or clusters are generally unreadable (Fig. 6 for ex), the same colour code should be used between figures and species for the same cell type (6a, S18)
-there is a foreign text on S1C.

In this manuscript, Chen et al. present a cross-species comparative study between mouse and macaque cochlear cell types. Nuclei were collected from cochlear epithelium, spiral ganglion, stria vascularis, spiral ligament, and other inner ear components including Reissner’s membrane, macrophages and osteoblasts. Through a series of computational comparative analyses, the authors demonstrated conserved and divergent features between mouse and macaque cochlea and cellular diversity in spiral ganglion neurons. This cochlear snRNAseq dataset from non-human primates is a tremendous feat and ultimately a step closer to understanding the pathophysiology of the inner ear in mammals. The major interest of the work by ‘Xin Chen et al.’ is that it provides a single cell transcriptomic dataset in a non-human primate essential to make sure the gene therapies designed in mice have a chance to be safe and to be rapidly translated to patients. The two major concerns that were raised have only been partially addressed:
i) The English writing was significantly improved making the manuscript more easily readable. However, there are still some language inaccuracies. More problematic is the fact that the authors did not increase the size of the text in the figures making many of them unreadable when printed on paper and requiring a zoom of 200-250% to be readable on the screen (see Fig.1d,2b,3b,3c,3d,3e,3f,4e,5b, 5c, 5g,6, supp fig1d,1e,1f, 1g,1h,2a,2b,2c,2d, 3a,3c,3d,3e,3g,3h, 4a, 4b, 12b,12c,12e,12g,13,14b,14c,14e,14g,15,17).
ii) Concerning the lack of additional cochlear transcriptomic knowledge, the improvements are limited probably owing to the filtering of the data obtained owing to the methodological set-up for several reasons: the limited number of macaques used, the use of aged tissue (compared to relatively young adult mice), and the use of single nucleus transcriptomics which provides more cells to the cost of sequencing depth. Despite these basic problems that are probably unsolvable, the authors could detect all key cochlear cell types and the data is potentially valuable as, to the best of my knowledge, no non-human primate cochlear transcriptome data is available yet. However, the authors should make clear the limitations of their data and not make overstatements. This point should be discussed extensively and in a balanced way.
Please find below more details:
1) The paragraph on cell diversity in the macaque cochlea is not very convincing owing to the limitations of the data mentioned above. The authors should be more careful in their conclusions as they are highly likely overstatements. Example: “glial cells in these two species differed in their transcriptional profiles”. The problem is the same with the section on the supporting cells : “this unexpected contrast between a small group of conserved genes and a large cohort of genes manifesting species-specific enrichment highlights the diversity of SC types across species”.
2) There is a similar problem in the “deafness associated genes across species section”.
The sentence “This indicates…that previously identified HL genes are mainly concentrated in HCs and are linked to HC functions” is a very likely overstatement. As mentioned in the review of the first submission, most if not all genetic forms of deafness have been replicated either from human to mouse or from mouse to human. Moreover, there are more and more examples of particular audiological signatures associated with specific genetic forms of deafness that have been uncovered in mice and that were confirmed subsequently in patients. So there is clearly a very close resemblance in the genetic architecture and function of mouse and human cochleae. It is therefore highly unlikely that the macaque diverged in a major different direction from mice and humans. The probable reasons for the observations of the authors is that they used adult/aging macaques and most of the pathogenic genes are involved in cochlear development, many of them being in hair cells but many others also in other cell types (see Fig. 7 from JeanP et al. 2023, PNAS). For example, it is puzzling that GJB2, a major gene underlying around 50% of the deafness forms does not show much expression and differential expression within cochlear cell types (see supp Fig. 17 of the authors) whereas it is known to be involved in many cochlear cell types.
3) Concerning the “sensory neuron diversity in the macaque cochlea”, the authors pinpoint the key proteins lacking in macaque SGNs (versus mice) like pou4f1 and LypD1. Did the authors find potential new markers specific of type1c macaque neurons (and more generally other neurons)? I think the information is not mentioned and it could potentially be beneficial to try to demonstrate the existence of type1C neurons on human tissue.
4) The discussion should balance more the conclusions in the light of the limitations linked to the small number of macaque replicates, the use of adult macaques compared to young mice, and the fact that single nucleus transcriptomic sequencing has less depth of sequencing. The authors should indicate the average depth of sequencing (number of read per cells) and also give statistics on mitochondrial genes in the material and methods.
5) I do not understand why the authors wanted absolutely to test for the presence of electromotility in a macaque. The electromotile property of OHCs can be monitored with a non invasive technique, called distortion products acoustic emissions (DPOAEs). DPOAEs are well characterized in mice and humans. They probably are too in many non-human primates (eg: Valero et al Hearing Research 2008, PMC2567920). In addition, mutations in the Prestin gene have been found to underly hearing loss in patients (ex: Toht et al, PMID: 17786286). I therefore do not understand why the authors wanted to make the point that prestin is indeed expressed by macaque OHCs and underlies electromotility. The sole detection of prestin was a good enough indication that they had found OHCs.
6) Why reanalyzing the data by (Jean P. et al, PNAS 2023)? I could not find the reason in the manuscript. I guess the reason is the use of a UMAP analysis rather than t-sne. If this is the case, the precision should be made in the manuscript. In addition, the citation of the paper should be made systematically for each panel in supp Fig.2 with a citation like (Jean P. et al, PNAS 2023) and not just saying “by PNAS”. This is important to make sure there is no ambiguity between the authors’ data and other studies’ data. In supp Fig. 3, the authors should clearly state in the figure legends that they are back to their own data, too.
7) In supplementary Fig 1f, the scheme appears to be a copy-paste of the scheme found in Fig. 1b of Jean P. et al, 2023 PNAS. Moreover, Fig.1a also corresponds to Fig 1b of of Jean P. et al, 2023 PNAS with an additional layer. There is absolutely no source cited in the legends of these figures. Could the authors make the corrections and also confirm that there are no other figures copy-pasted from any other article/journal?
8) Other points:
-line94: ‘preferentially’ should be removed
-line 100: “extreme’ should be removed
-Line 112: “gene therapeutics” would better read “gene therapies”
-line 127: the adjective “non human primate” could be added to “constructing a cell atlas”.
-line 142: “in 1-year-old and 11-year old macaques” should read “in a 1-year-old and an 11-year old macaques”
-line 151: “These results strongly implicate” would better read as “These results shows”?
-line 156: “Oterferlin” should read otoferlin
- line 198: Maybe remind for the general reader what are Remak bundles.
-line 265: “to integrate the mouse” should read “to integrate our mouse” to avoid any ambiguity.
-Supp figures 6 and 7 are nice in that they can be put in parallel. However, the authors removed the GFAP from the mouse analysis. Why is it so whereas all other markers are exactly the same between macaque and mouse data?
-Please add the number of nuclei for each UMAP on the figures.
-Supplementary Fig. 17: lacking a scalebar
-Please verify on all the figures that a scale bar is present and readable

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Unraveling the intricate composition and function of the cochlea is paramount to comprehending the mechanisms underlying sound perception and the pathogenesis of auditory disorders. The mammalian cochlea displays a highly organized structure, which contributes to the diversity and complexity of auditory processing. However, the cellular intricacies in non-human primates remain largely unexplored. In the present study, we employed high-throughput transcriptomic sequencing to profile over 36,701 nuclei across virtually all cochlear cell types in both juvenile and adult Macaca fascicularis at single-cell resolution. Our analysis unveiled remarkable heterogeneity both across and within cell types. Despite a largely conserved cellular composition of the cochlea between mouse and macaque species, glial cells exhibited substantial species-specific diversity, while hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons with specialized transcriptional programs were well-mapped onto their murine counterparts, underscoring the similarities that persist despite evolutionary divergence. Furthermore, we constructed a disease map associated with hearing loss, establishing this transcriptomic atlas of the macaque cochlea as an indispensable resource for future investigations in both human and non-human primates.

---

## Introduction

The cochlea, a coiled structure situated in the inner ear, performs unique biophysical functions in vertebrates and serves as the primary sound transducer. Airborne pressure waves induce fluid-based traveling waves at the base of the cochlea, which propagate towards the apex within the scala vestibuli. These waves progressively vibrate the spiral duct in the scala media and subsequently travel back toward the base in the scala tympani1. During this complex fluctuation process, the sensory epithelium lining the floor of the scala media, known as the cochlear epithelium, perceives mechanical stimuli and transduces physical signals to neurons2. The cochlear epithelium comprises two types of mechanosensory hair cells (HCs), namely inner HCs and outer HCs, and at least six types of associated glia-like supporting cells (SCs). The scarcity of HCs and SCs in mammals, with approximately 700 inner HCs and 2000 outer HCs in mice3, and around 15,000 HCs in the human cochlea3, poses significant challenges in investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying the development and physiology of this organ. Furthermore, the vulnerability and sensitivity of cochlear cells, particularly those in the epithelial tissue, coupled with the calcification of the temporal bone in juvenile and adult stages, render cochlear dissection an exceptionally arduous task.

Damage or degeneration of the cochlea can lead to irreversible HC loss in mammals4,5, with hereditary hearing loss (HL) being the most common disabling sensorineural disorder. The majority of genes known to be associated with deafness are expressed in specific cochlear cell types, such as HCs, and these genes often affect the mechanoelectrical transduction components in the hair bundles that are critical for sound perception, including Cib2 (calcium and integrin-binding family member 2), Tmie (transmembrane protein), and Tmc1/2 (transmembrane channel-like protein 1/2). Other genes, such as GJB2 (connexin-26), are expressed in several types of SCs6. However, a comprehensive disease map of deafness genes in non-human primates remains elusive. Gene therapy strategies, primarily based on the adeno-associated virus delivery system, are increasingly being tested in mouse models that mimic human deafness. Nevertheless, it is imperative to optimize the safety and efficacy of gene therapies in larger animal models, such as non-human primates, for advanced preclinical trials due to species-specific differences in physiology and anatomy between mice and humans.

Over the past two decades, developmental biologists have made significant strides in uncovering the cellular and genetic processes that regulate the formation of this remarkable structure, including the major axes of cochlear development7,8, HC fate determination and trans-differentiation9,10, and the identification and function of the mechanoelectrical transduction complex11,12. In rodents, the sensory epithelium and spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) remain immature prior to and at birth, undergoing remodeling and maturation around postnatal days (P) 2113,14, concurrent with the regression of the greater epithelial ridge, detachment of the tectorial membrane, and the formation of the endocochlear potential15,16. Recent advances in microfluidic-based single-cell/single-nucleus transcriptomic approaches, which enable the capture of large numbers of cells, have facilitated the development of cell atlases of the mouse cochlea from embryonic to adult stages17–19. However, a comprehensive cell transcriptomic atlas of the cochlea in non-human primates has yet to be undertaken20. Given their evolutionary proximity to humans, constructing a non-human primate cell atlas as a reference for the cochlea is a critical step in advancing our understanding of human auditory physiology, disease, and aging.

In the present study, we utilized juvenile and adult Macaca fascicularis cochleae to generate a high-quality single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas. This map revealed remarkable cellular diversity in the spiral ganglion region, particularly among glial cells. Furthermore, we identified conserved and divergent features between the mouse and macaque cochlea. We anticipate that this atlas will be invaluable for understanding evolutionary innovations in the mammalian cochlea and for developing organoid models and gene therapy of human diseases associated with deafness.

---

## Results

A cell type atlas of the macaque cochlea
To determine the cellular composition of the macaque cochlea, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; Droplet-based 10× Genomics) on 36,701 nuclei after quality control, doublet removal, and filtering (Fig. 1a–d and Supplementary Fig. 1a–c; for details see “Method”). We profiled the entire cochlea, with nuclei sampled from the cochlear epithelium, spiral ganglion, stria vascularis, spiral ligament, and other tissues, including macrophages and pericytes, in a 1-, 5-, and 11-year-old macaques across approximately juvenile and adult stages (Supplementary Figs. 1–3b, c).

To fine-tune the characterization of macaque cochlear cell types, we first utilized the published single-nucleus and single-cell transcriptome of murine cochleae as a reference for assessing well-established marker genes used for manual cell-type annotation (Supplementary Fig. 4). These gene markers used in the referenced dataset have been thoroughly validated in the murine cochlea across juvenile and adult periods19. We found that our in-house single-nucleus sequencing data of the murine cochlea at P25 exhibited approximately similar cellular diversity comparable to the referenced dataset from Jean et al.19 (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6) and observed accurate cell-type mapping onto our macaque cochleae (Fig. 1d, e and Supplementary Figs. 1d, e, g, h and 2a, b). However, some differences exist as circulating cells including erythrocytes, neutrophils, B cells, T cells, NK cells, monocytes, and mast cells are undetectable in our in-house dataset compared to Jean et al.’s dataset19 (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Figs. 1, 2 and 5). We reasoned that it is likely due to cochlear dissection process for single-nucleus suspension we used, which was different from Jean et al.19.

By using a support vector machine classifier trained on the macaque cells, we find strong correspondence between the transcriptomic signatures of the sensory organ cell types in macaques and mice underscoring a highly conserved molecular identity between macaque and murine species (Supplementary Fig. 3d), as well as high quality and accuracy within these cell types (Supplementary Figs. 1f, i, 2c, and 5c, g). Moreover, our atlas also displays five main cell-type ensembles (Supplementary Fig. 3c) as noted previously19. The cell ensembles of the neurosensory epithelium, for instance, consist of SCs (defined by OTOG expression) and HCs (defined by MYO7A expression; Supplementary Fig. 3c). For further validation of these sequencing data, we applied immunofluorescence assays to confirm the localization of selectively the most differentially expressed genes. CALB1 encoding calbindin, a hair cell marker9, is localized in both inner and outer HCs. Otoferlin (OTOF), an inner HC marker21, is exclusively present in inner HCs when HCs become mature. CALB2 encoding calretinin, a calcium-binding protein, is illustrated as localized in SGNs22–24. All these immunolabeling experiments also exhibited similar cell-type-specific localization in both species (Fig. 1f). Furthermore, RNAscopeTM in situ hybridization also confirm the spatial expression patterns of ANXA1 in root cells and spindle cells as well as OTOGL in HCs and SCs (Supplementary Fig. 3a).

Furthermore, we were able to map the unique biological functions of each cell type via gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of these highly variable genes (Supplementary Data 1), revealing remarkably similar biological functions across species. For example, sensory processing of sound mapped to HCs, actin filament-based processes to SCs, modulation of chemical synaptic transmission to SGNs, myelination to Schwann cells, and cell junction organization to marginal stria cells. Collectively, we constructed an accessible cellular taxonomy of the juvenile and adult macaque cochlea, revealing an evolutionarily conserved, highly specialized sensory organ across mammalian species based on a clustering analysis for identifying cell types of cochlear cells using the expression of canonical marker genes in mice.

Auditory receptors in macaque cochlea
HCs with unique mechanical sensory properties in the auditory system play a crucial role in sound transduction. To gain comprehensive insights into their molecular identities compared to mouse species, we integrated our macaque and mouse single-nucleus data separately using the single-cell variational inference (scVI) method25 (Supplementary Fig. 6) and subset the HC population based on the unique expression of the HC marker MYO7A/Myo7a (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). We observed a strong correspondence between the transcriptomic signatures of the HC lineages in macaques and mice, as mature/terminal marker genes26–28 (OHC: SLC26A5/Slc26a5, KCNQ4/Kcnq4 and PCP4/Ocm; IHC: SLC17A8/Slc17a8, CALB2/Calb2, and ATP2A3/Atp2a3) are selectively enriched in these two subtypes (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 7). The motor protein PRESTIN was precisely localized in the OHC basolateral membrane in both species (Fig. 2b, c and Supplementary Fig. 7) and OHCs in macaque species exhibited the biophysical feature of motility evoked by electrical stimuli (Fig. 2d and Movie S1). Furthermore, well-characterized transcriptional regulators that specify and maintain the fate of OHCs and IHCs, including IKZF29 (which encodes IKAROS family zinc finger 2) and TBX210,29 (which encodes T-box transcription factor 2), were strongly expressed in HCs across species (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 7). These findings suggest that HCs in the cochlea of both species might share conserved gene regulatory machinery.

Glial cell diversity in the macaque cochlea
In the mouse cochlea, glial cells exhibit spatial and functional heterogeneity and can be categorized into three distinct subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 8): satellite glial cells (SGSs), myelinating Schwann cells (MSCs), and non-myelinating Schwann cells (NMSCs). Unique marker genes for these subtypes have been well-established in mice30. To investigate this diversity in the macaque cochlea, we sub-clustered glial cells into three subtypes (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 8c). Similar to murine glial types, macaque glial cells displayed region-specific differences in the spiral ganglion region, including cells enveloping sensory neurons (SGCs), cells wrapping around axons forming myelin (MSCs), and Remak bundles (NMSCs), as demonstrated by immunostaining of the pan-glial marker MBP for glial localization (Fig. 3b, c). However, we were unable to map macaque glial subtypes using several defined markers (SCN7A, encoding an atypical Na-sensitive Na-channel that marks NMSCs30,31; NCAMP, encoding a non-compact myelin-associated protein that marks MSCs30,32; and IGFBP6, encoding the insulin-like growth factor binding protein 6 that marks SGCs30) that have been validated in mice30 (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 8b and d). To further harmonize both species’ glial subtypes, we changed different highly variable genes (hvgs) imputed for anchoring and found that varying the number of hvgs did not affect the species or cell-type mixings in the manifold embedding spaces, and we still obtained a relatively stable high-level structure for the data manifold (Supplementary Fig. 9a–c). This might suggest that there is relatively high transcriptomic divergence in peripheral glial cell types between macaques and mice. Indeed, these cluster pairs showed relatively low classification accuracy with various cells showing overlaps (Supplementary Fig. 9d) as well as cell mixing upon multiple integrative method we used for cross-species integration (Supplementary Fig. 10). For example, we found that the pan-astrocyte marker GFAP showed region-specific localization in mouse MSCs but was more diverse in macaque glial cells, including cells engulfing SGNs and cells parallel to axons (Fig. 3e).

In the central nervous system (CNS), astrocytes play auxiliary roles in neuron development, synapse formation and elimination, potassium homeostasis, and blood-brain barrier function33–35. A recent single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of the peripheral sensory system revealed that glial cells in the mouse cochlea share many core glial signature genes with radial glial cells and astrocytes in the CNS30. To explore potential functional implications, we plotted genes associated with astrocyte function and compared the molecular profiles of glial cells in both species (Fig. 3f). Our analysis revealed several apparent species-specific gene expression patterns related to astrocyte functions. For instance, glial cells in mice showed predominant expression of Na+-K+-ATPase channels (higher levels of ATP1B1, ATP1A1, and ATP1A2), while glial subtypes in macaques displayed higher levels of glutamate receptors (GRIA2 and GR1K2), potentially associated with potassium buffering. Regarding debris clearance, CLU36 and LRP137 were more prominently expressed in macaque glial cells, while MEGF1037 and MERTK37 were more abundant in mouse glial cells. Consistent with these findings, our RNAscopeTM results suggest that peripheral glial cells in macaque could be divided into two main types (Fig. 3j): GRIA2-positive SGSs predominantly located in the modiolus region (Fig. 3g), and CLU-/GRIA2-positive or CLU-positive Schwann cells distributed along the outer modiolar region as neuronal fibers project into both cochlear epithelium (Fig. 3h) and cochlear nuclei (Fig. 3i). These spatial distributions were generally consistent with the sequencing data showing widespread GRIA2 expression in macaque glial cells and selective CLU enrichment in GC_1/GC_3 clusters (Fig. 3f).

While we observed differences in gene expression patterns between species, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the technical limitations of snRNA sequencing. Further validation would be needed to determine whether these molecular differences reflect genuine functional divergence in cochlear glial cells across species.

Sensory neuron diversity in the macaque cochlea
We next investigated the diversity of SGNs. Defined by canonical markers in mice23,24 (Supplementary Fig. 11), 955 SGNs in macaques can be re-clustered into type I/II subclasses and subdivided into four subtypes with distinct expression patterns (Fig. 4a, b and Supplementary Fig. 12). However, subtle differences were observed in macaque sensory neurons (Fig. 4c, d and Supplementary Fig. 12c). TH expression was preferentially enriched only in mouse type II neurons, and the type IC marker genes POU4F1 and LYPD1 were specifically expressed in mouse type IC neurons. Interestingly, we found that, unlike mouse SGNs, expression of the type IB marker CALB1 was enriched in macaque type II neurons (Fig. 4b, c and Supplementary Fig. 13). Immunolabeling of CALB1 with type II markers, including GATA3 and PRPH proteins, confirmed that CALB1 protein is co-localized with these two type II SGN markers, indicating that CALB1 is a macaque-specific marker for type II sensory neurons (Fig. 4d).

Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) analysis identified a cohort of conserved transcription factors (TFs) that were share either in type I or type II SGNs in both species (Fig. 4e, g). Among them, some have been previously reported, such as PROX138, RUNX139, and SMAD122. For example, RUNX1 is essential for type IC SGN specification. Immunolabeling and RNASCOPE assay confirmed these TFs selectively expressed in SGN subtypes (Fig. 4f, h). Additionally, we found primate-specific TFs PBX3 particularly expressed in type II SGNs (Fig. 4i). Gene set enrichment analysis showed that the key TF PBX3 is involved in GO terms related to neuron development (Fig. 4j). Immunofluorescence staining confirmed that the PBX3 protein is localized in the cell nucleus of macaque SGNs, probably as a specific subtype, but not in mouse SGNs (Fig. 4k). However, future experiments should be conducted to determine if PBX3 plays primate-specific roles in SGNs.

The similarity and specificity of expression profiles in the cochlear epithelium
We focused on the cochlear epithelium, also known as the organ of Corti, which is a highly specialized structure for sound detection and transduction40–42. To explore cross-species similarities and differences in the cochlear epithelium at different taxonomic levels, we employed mutiple label-transfer algorithms (scVI, CCA, and Symphany) to integrate our in-house mouse cochlear epithelium clusters as references and projected the 10, 870 macaque single-nucleus transcriptomes onto them based on their distances in their joint-embedding spaces (Fig. 5a, b and Supplementary Fig. 14; see “Methods”), resulting in highly overlapped anchoring identity (Fig. 5c). Additionally, label transfer-based integrated cell types exhibited highly similar transcriptomes (Fig. 5d, e) though we found CC_ISC_OSC and IBC_IPh_HeC varied across species, suggesting their species-specificity.

Further analysis of the expression of gene families across cluster pairs indicated that, as demonstrated in other systems43–45, certain families, such as G protein-coupled receptors and TFs (especially the zinc finger types), displayed cell type-specific expression patterns in the cochlear epithelium (Fig. 5f, g). This suggests that zinc finger type TFs might function as markers of cochlear epithelium identity in both species. Indeed, our immunolabeling or RNAscopeTM assay of selective TFs (GATA3, IKZF2, PBX3, and NR2F2) showed similar expression patterns across species (Fig. 5h, i). However, a supervised learning task for testing the ability of gene-sets related to signaling, ion channels, and cell adhesion to distinguish cochlear epithelium consensus types showed similar classification performance when trained and tested within species (r-value greater than 1.12) but declined sharply across species (60% in macaques and mice; Fig. 5j). Altogether, these results indicate that evolutionary conservation might be maintained by combined TF codes, while species-specific adaptation might be driven by species-enriched genes (either TFs or effector genes).

Mapping deafness-associated genes across species
To further examine our dataset and gain deep insights into the cross-species expression profile of genes related to hereditary hearing loss (HHL), we mapped HHL-related genes (https://hereditaryhearingloss.org, updated on 02/17/2022) categorized into four types: autosomal dominant nonsyndromic HL (48 genes), autosomal recessive nonsyndromic HL (74 genes), syndromic HL (41 genes), and X-linked nonsyndromic/age/noise/cisplatin-related HL (46 genes) in our databases for systematic characterization of their expression profiles. It is important to note that genes linked to age, noise, and cisplatin-related HL by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have not been extensively investigated in the inner ear (GWAS Catalog (ebi.ac.uk)). Through the overall examination of HL-related gene expression in the macaque, we observed that the majority of these genes exhibit cell-type-specific expression patterns (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 15). For instance, POU4F3—a well-established deafness gene—is predominantly expressed in HCs, with its mutations known to cause DFNA15, a common autosomal dominant hearing loss disorder. The gene Gjb2, which encodes connexin 26 for gap junctions, is broadly expressed in SCs and cells of the lateral wall. Mutations in Gjb2 are associated with both congenital HL and later-onset deafness. Notably, our data demonstrate highly conserved expression patterns across 1-, 5-, and 11-year-old macaques, further validating the robustness of our dataset. Cross-species comparative analysis reveals that deafness-associated genes are evolutionarily conserved between macaques and mice, sharing analogous expression profiles. Together, this analysis revealed the cross-species distributions of HL-related genes within the whole cochlear map. Given the close evolutionary proximity of macaque to humans, establishing this atlas holds significant implications for advancing research on human auditory pathologies.

---

## Methods

Animals and ethical compliance
All experiments involving macaques (Macaca fascicularis) were conducted in strict accordance with the guidelines set forth by the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International (AAALAC) for the ethical treatment of non-human primates. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the ethical committee of the State Key Laboratory of Primate Biomedical Research. For the purpose of single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq), cochleae from one 1-year-old male, two 5-year-old male, and one 11-year-old female macaque were utilized. Immunostaining experiments were performed using cochleae from three 5-year-old male and one 11-year-old male macaque. Electromotility recordings were obtained from one 1-year-old male macaque. All animals were housed in facilities that meet the standards of the AAALAC, and their well-being was closely monitored throughout the study.

C57BL/6J mice used in this study were purchased from GenePharmtech Co., Ltd. and housed in a standard specific pathogen free environment. Mice of either sex aged postnatal days 21 to 25 were used in this study with no obvious sex phenotype observed. All mice were housed under controlled conditions, including room temperature (23±3°C), relative humidity (55±5%), and a 12-h light/dark cycle. During the feeding process, all mice were provided with sterile water and nutrient-balanced feed. Additionally, each cage was equipped with non-toxic and harmless bedding.

Macaque RNA-seq, quality control, and clustering
Sample collection.
